articles.title: Mark Street Roadworks Scheduled for 24 October 2026
articles.excerpt: Roadworks on Mark Street in Rochdale will result in a temporary closure from midnight to 11.59pm on Saturday, 24 October 2026, affecting traffic flow in the area.
articles.content_html:
Mark Street in Rochdale will be temporarily closed on Saturday, 24 October 2026, from midnight until 11.59pm. The closure will affect the section of Mark Street between its junctions with Halifax Road and Athol Street.

During this period, no waiting will be permitted in the affected area. Motorists are advised to plan their journeys accordingly, as the closure may impact traffic flow on nearby roads, including Halifax Road, Davyhulme Street, and Athol Street.

This roadwork is part of ongoing maintenance efforts by Rochdale Borough Council to improve local infrastructure. Residents and commuters are encouraged to check the Rochdale Borough Council website for updates on the roadworks and any further announcements regarding local traffic changes.

For more information, including a map of the roadworks, visit the Rochdale Borough Council website. The council also provides a map of roadworks across Greater Manchester for those needing to navigate around the closures.

articles.title: Rochdale Camera Clubs Welcome New Members to Explore Local Photography
articles.excerpt: Local camera clubs are inviting new members to join and explore the area's diverse wildlife, landscapes, and architecture. The Rochdale & District Camera Club meets weekly to foster a love for photography among enthusiasts.
articles.content_html:
Photographic enthusiasts in Rochdale have the opportunity to join local camera clubs that celebrate the art of photography. The Rochdale & District Camera Club, which meets every Tuesday evening at Syke Community Base & Methodist Chapel, is particularly keen to welcome new members. The club aims to bring together individuals with varying levels of experience and interests, fostering a supportive environment for all.

The club's activities include a mix of visiting speakers, practical sessions, competitions, and members' presentations. Recent sessions have covered topics such as portraiture, image editing, and creative techniques like light painting. The club emphasises the importance of getting out with a camera to capture the beauty of the local area, which is rich in wildlife, landscapes, and architecture.

Martyn Slater, a member of the club, highlighted the diverse photographic opportunities available in Rochdale. He noted that whether one's passion lies in capturing scenery or sports, there is something for everyone. The club encourages photographers to learn from each other and to enhance their skills through shared experiences and challenges.

For those interested in joining the Rochdale & District Camera Club, meetings are held every Tuesday evening, providing a welcoming space for both novice and experienced photographers. This initiative not only promotes photography as a hobby but also helps to strengthen community ties through shared interests.

articles.title: Final Opportunity to View Hidden Documents and Artefacts in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Rochdale's Local Studies Centre and Square Gallery are showcasing previously unseen documents and artefacts until the end of September, highlighting the town's rich heritage.
articles.content_html:
Time is running out for residents to view a unique collection of documents and artefacts that have been hidden in Rochdale's archives. The display, which is part of the Unlocking Collections project, is currently available for viewing at the Rochdale Local Studies Centre and the Square Gallery on Rochdale Town Hall Square until the end of September.

The project, a collaboration between Rochdale Local Studies and the Co-operative Heritage Trust, involved ten volunteers who meticulously searched through various documents, donations, and purchases that reflect the town's heritage. Their efforts have culminated in an exhibition that brings local stories to life through artwork inspired by the archives.

Rochdale Local Studies Centre shared on social media, thanking the volunteers for their creativity and hard work. The exhibition showcases the innovative and radical history of Rochdale, with documents that have accumulated over time through generous contributions from the community.

Residents and visitors are encouraged to take advantage of this final opportunity to explore the rich history of Rochdale before the exhibition concludes. For more information, visit the Rochdale Local Studies Centre or the Square Gallery.

articles.title: Are there really fairies in Healey Dell?
articles.excerpt: The rocky cleft known locally as the Fairies’ Chapel is a real landscape feature with a long history of storytelling — but the supernatural claims sit in folklore, not the council’s records.
articles.summary: The rocky cleft known locally as the Fairies’ Chapel is a real landscape feature with a long history of storytelling — but the supernatural claims sit in folklore, not the council’s records.
articles.body:
Healey Dell’s Fairies’ Chapel is one of those place‑names that makes you stop on the riverside path and look twice. Tucked under the dramatic Victorian viaduct where the River Spodden squeezes through a narrow gorge known locally as “the Thrutch”, a small waterfall and water‑worn cavity in the rock have been likened by generations of visitors to a pulpit, seats and an alcove — and that resemblance is the simple, documented reason for the name.

What is documented

Healey Dell is managed and promoted as a nature reserve by Rochdale Borough Council and is an established local attraction for walkers, schools and families. The borough’s public information describes the site as a beauty spot rich in industrial archaeology — mills, lodges, waterways and the disused Lancashire & Yorkshire Railway viaduct that towers over the Dell. The viaduct itself is recorded on the National Heritage List for England (listed Grade II), confirming the area’s clear industrial and built‑heritage significance. Local guides and the Healey Dell Heritage Centre also record that the river carved a hollow in the rock that early visitors described as church‑like; those water‑worn shapes are a natural feature, the product of erosion over long periods and of particular flood events that changed the valley’s appearance. The Heritage Centre’s own guides and trail maps point to the Fairies’ Chapel as a named point of interest in the reserve and explain the site’s mix of nature, industrial remains and local story‑telling.

One important, verifiable event helps explain why the Chapel looks different now from how 19th‑century writers described it: an extreme storm on 4 July 1838 (commonly called the July Flood) caused severe flooding through the Spodden valley, washed away bridges and damaged mills — contemporary and later local records note that parts of the rock cavity known as the Fairies’ Chapel were altered or destroyed by that event. That is a documented landscape change, not a tale.

What the stories say

The supernatural side of Healey Dell belongs to folklore. Local and Victorian‑era accounts collected in guidebooks, verse and oral tradition mix fairy lore, a so‑called Fairy Queen, tales of witches turned to stone and even a loose connection to regional Robin Hood‑type stories in popular retellings. These stories treat the rock cavity as a “chapel” for the fair folk and describe meetings, prophecies and magical happenings. Local interpretation and visitor materials at the Heritage Centre celebrate these traditions as part of Healey Dell’s cultural heritage.

What we can — and cannot — verify

We can verify the place‑name, the nature‑reserve status, the existence of the viaduct and the effects of the 1838 flood from council records and heritage listings. We can also verify that Victorian and later local guides recorded fairy legends associated with the site and that the Heritage Centre re‑publishes these tales as part of its local‑history interpretation.

What we cannot verify are claims of actual supernatural events. There are no official records, inspections or historical documents that prove the existence of fairies, a Fairy King, or witches being turned to stone in Healey Dell. Those elements belong to oral tradition, local verse and the imaginative accounts that have grown up around the striking rock shapes. When guides or storytellers link Healey Dell to prophetic fairy queens or dramatic magical episodes, they are recounting folklore rather than reporting a verifiable historical event.

Why the mix matters

Places like Healey Dell matter precisely because they gather both stones and stories. The geology and industrial archaeology give the Dell its real, provable history; the fairy tales give it local colour and a living tradition that attracts visitors and sparks imagination — including events, trail materials and seasonal storytelling organised by the Heritage Centre. For readers: you can enjoy the Fairies’ Chapel as a quiet, atmospheric spot shaped by water and time, and as a place where Rochdale’s folklore is still remembered. But if you want official facts about land management, listed structures, or landscape change, those belong to council and heritage records; the fairies remain, for now, in the stories.

articles.title: Why Rochdale says “cruckle”
articles.excerpt: How a short, local verb — to “cruckle” your ankle — links Rochdale speech to an older northern‑English dialect family and why locals still claim it as their own.
articles.summary: How a short, local verb — to “cruckle” your ankle — links Rochdale speech to an older northern‑English dialect family and why locals still claim it as their own.
articles.body:
If you grew up in parts of Rochdale you’ll recognise the line: “I cruckled me ankle.” Locally, to “cruckle” means to roll, twist or go over on your ankle — that sharp, hobbling stumble you can sometimes walk off but that still makes you wince.

That everyday meaning is not just neighbourhood folklore. A recent perceptual‑dialect study of Greater Manchester (draw‑a‑map / keywords method) collected hundreds of free comments from residents and found “cruckle” listed among the words people explicitly associate with Rochdale speech, alongside other locally salient terms such as guinnel (ginnel) and “broad.” In other words, people across the region perceive cruckle as a recognisable Rochdale marker rather than as a random slang item.

But cruckle is not a brand‑new invention restricted to a single street. Historical dialect scholarship records older and related forms — most commonly crookle — with senses that cover bending, making crooked, stooping or hobbling. Joseph Wright’s English Dialect Dictionary (late 19th/early 20th century) collects crookle and similar headwords from northern and midland counties in senses that naturally extend to limping or going wrong with a foot. Those historical attestations show the word belongs to a wider northern‑English dialect family rather than springing up overnight in Rochdale.

The wider picture is supported by Scots and northern dialect material. The Dictionaries of the Scots Language records cognate variants (kruggle, cruggle, cruckle, krukel) with meanings such as to crouch, huddle or bend; the entry brings together quotations dating from the late 19th and early 20th centuries. These cognates point to a common root (crook/krug‑) and the frequentative/imitative suffix ‑le that turns roots into verbs meaning repeated or small actions (so crook → crookle/cruckle).

So why does Rochdale feel particularly identified with the term? Two complementary facts explain it. First, ordinary use: people in and around Rochdale still use cruckle in the ankle‑sense, keeping the word alive in everyday speech. Second, folk‑awareness: perceptual research shows locals and neighbouring Greater Manchester residents explicitly list cruckle when asked to name words that signal Rochdale speech. That combination — continued usage plus shared recognition — is what gives the word its local badge value.

Is cruckle unique to Rochdale? Strictly speaking no. Dialect records show related forms across northern England and in Scots dialects, so the root and pattern are regional. But uniqueness in dialects is often a matter of degree. Many neighbouring places will have similar old verbs or different local favourites; what sets Rochdale’s claim apart is the particular survival and social visibility of cruckle there. In short: the etymological family is wider, but the modern reputation and everyday ankle‑sense are strongly tied to Rochdale in people’s minds.

Why does this matter beyond trivia? Small, everyday words such as cruckle are useful signals for dialect researchers because they reveal both living speech practice (who says what, where) and folk perception (which words people think define a place). Contemporary perceptual methods — asking residents to draw or list the words they associate with local speech — combine with archival lexicography to show how old dialect vocabulary is kept alive (or lost) and how language becomes a local identity marker.

If you’re from Rochdale, cruckle is one of those short pieces of speech that can prompt a knowing nod; if you’re visiting, try it after a tumble in a ginnel and you’ll soon find out whether you’ve landed in the right place. For readers who want to check the research behind this piece, the perceptual study and the historical dictionary records are publicly accessible and show both the modern association with Rochdale and the word’s wider dialect history.

articles.title: Rochdale AFC Women Exit FA Cup After 3-1 Defeat to Nantwich Town
articles.excerpt: Nantwich Town Women secured a place in the next round of the WFA Cup with a 3-1 victory over Rochdale AFC at the Crown Oil Arena on September 20, 2026.
articles.content_html:
Nantwich Town Women progressed to the next round of the Women’s FA Cup following a 3-1 victory against Rochdale AFC at the Crown Oil Arena on September 20, 2026. The Dabbers started the match strongly, dominating possession and creating several scoring opportunities.

Nantwich goalkeeper Connie made crucial saves to maintain their lead as they capitalised on their early momentum. The visitors' attacking play proved effective, allowing them to secure a comfortable win against their opponents.

Rochdale Women struggled to find their rhythm throughout the match, managing to score only once despite their efforts. The defeat means they will exit the competition at this stage, while Nantwich Town Women will look forward to their next fixture in the tournament.

The victory marks an important milestone for Nantwich Town Women, who will now prepare for the upcoming round of the WFA Cup, aiming to build on this success in their future matches.
